ai.definition: Homomorphic Encryption Processing is a cryptographic method that allows computations to be carried out on data in its encrypted form. The result of these computations, when decrypted, matches the result of performing the same operations on the plaintext.
ai.howItWorks: Homomorphic encryption works by applying mathematical operations to ciphertexts (encrypted data) such that they reflect equivalent operations on the corresponding plaintexts (unencrypted data). This is achieved through complex mathematical transformations and algorithms that ensure security while enabling computation on encrypted data.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional encryption methods require data to be decrypted before any processing can occur, which poses significant risks in terms of privacy and security. Homomorphic encryption allows for secure computations without exposing the underlying plaintext, addressing these concerns in scenarios such as cloud computing and medical data analysis.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and implementing complex cryptographic algorithms that are computationally intensive. This process requires advanced mathematical expertise and robust software development practices.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing encryption schemes, testing their security and efficiency, and integrating them into existing systems or cloud environments. It also involves creating secure protocols for key management and ensuring compliance with privacy regulations.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the computational overhead of performing operations on encrypted data, which can be high due to the complexity of homomorphic encryption algorithms. Additionally, there are costs associated with software development, testing, and maintaining security standards.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Homomorphic Encryption Processing is expected to see significant growth as privacy concerns continue to rise in various industries, particularly cloud computing and healthcare.
ai.regulation: Regulations around data privacy and encryption vary by region. Homomorphic encryption must comply with local laws such as GDPR or HIPAA, which may require additional compliance efforts.
ai.risks: Risks include potential vulnerabilities in the encryption algorithms themselves, performance overhead due to computational complexity, and challenges in key management and secure implementation.
ai.profitability: Profitability is uncertain but could be significant if homomorphic encryption becomes widely adopted. However, current limitations in efficiency and widespread adoption pose challenges for immediate financial returns.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving the efficiency of homomorphic encryption schemes to make them more practical for real-world applications, as well as addressing security concerns through ongoing research and refinement.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking. Computational processes require significant power but are less intensive than traditional data processing methods.

glossary.def: A form of encryption that allows computations to be carried out on ciphertext, which generates an encrypted result that can be decrypted to match the result of operations performed on the plaintext.
Encrypted data that is unreadable without a decryption key.
Unencrypted data that is readable and understandable in its original form.
The process of generating, storing, distributing, revoking, and destroying cryptographic keys used for encryption and decryption.

subsystems.name: Encoder
subsystems.role: packs ordinary numbers into the algebraic slots a ciphertext can hold.

subsystems.name: Ciphertext ring arithmetic
subsystems.role: the core object: polynomials in a ring, each carrying deliberate 'noise' that hides the message.

subsystems.name: Evaluation engine
subsystems.role: performs addition, multiplication and rotation directly on ciphertexts.

subsystems.name: Noise manager
subsystems.role: keeps the accumulated noise low enough that decryption still works.

subsystems.name: Key material
subsystems.role: everything the client generates and shares so a server can compute without decrypting.
parts: secret key (stays with the data owner)
evaluation keys, which can run to hundreds of megabytes

subsystems.name: Accelerator layer
subsystems.role: makes the huge polynomial arithmetic affordable.

subsystems.name: Compiler and parameter chooser
subsystems.role: turns a normal program into a depth-limited arithmetic circuit with valid security parameters.
parts: polynomial approximations of functions like sigmoid or square root
security-parameter selection per the HomomorphicEncryption.org standard

buildSteps.title: Pick the scheme
buildSteps.detail: Exact-integer schemes suit counting and database lookups; approximate schemes suit statistics and machine learning; bit-level schemes suit comparisons and control logic. The choice fixes what the rest of the system can express.

buildSteps.title: Choose security parameters
buildSteps.detail: Select the polynomial ring dimension and modulus chain so the noise problem stays hard for an attacker, using the community security standard rather than guesswork.

buildSteps.title: Generate keys on the client
buildSteps.detail: Create a secret key, a public key and the evaluation keys a server will need for multiplication and rotation. Large key sizes are the price of letting someone else compute on your data.

buildSteps.title: Encode and encrypt
buildSteps.detail: Pack many values into one ciphertext at once. This batching is what turns an impossibly slow idea into something sometimes workable.

buildSteps.title: Express the computation as a circuit
buildSteps.detail: Rewrite the algorithm using only additions and multiplications, and approximate any other mathematical function with a polynomial. Every multiplication consumes 'depth', so the circuit must be shallow.

buildSteps.title: Evaluate on the server
buildSteps.detail: The server multiplies, adds and rotates ciphertexts it cannot read, periodically relinearising and switching moduli down the chain to control noise. It sees only meaningless polynomials.

buildSteps.title: Refresh with bootstrapping
buildSteps.detail: When noise gets too close to the decryption threshold, the server runs the client's own decryption routine homomorphically to produce a fresh, low-noise ciphertext of the same value. This is the most expensive step.

buildSteps.title: Return and decrypt
buildSteps.detail: The encrypted result goes back to the data owner, who alone can decrypt it. The server never held a key that could read the input or the output.

prerequisites.why: the security of the whole scheme rests on the hardness of recovering a secret from noisy linear equations.
multiplying thousand-term polynomials is the dominant cost; without a fast transform it is hopeless.
discovered in 2009, it turned a theoretical curiosity into a general technique, but it still dominates runtime.
FPGAs, GPUs and experimental ASICs cut the overhead by large factors, but none is yet a commodity product.
shared security parameters and open libraries are needed before auditors and regulators will accept results.

pathway.milestone: narrow high-value uses: private database lookup, private information retrieval, encrypted similarity search and pilot analytics in cloud and health settings
pathway.unlocks: proof that the technique can ship inside real products when the computation is small.

pathway.milestone: purpose-built accelerators plus better compilers bring realistic workloads within reach
pathway.unlocks: encrypted machine-learning inference and query processing at practical cost.

pathway.milestone: threshold and multi-key variants, where several parties share the decryption key
pathway.unlocks: joint computation across organisations that trust neither each other nor the cloud.

pathway.milestone: hybrid designs pairing encrypted computation with hardware enclaves and secure multi-party computation
pathway.unlocks: routine processing of regulated data — medical, financial, governmental — without ever exposing it in the clear.
